title: Three Treasures 1
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up the Pali chant of the three refuges, sung at the end of the day in the Soto Zen tradition, along with the tenth precept, not defaming the three treasures. Starting from the astronaut's view of the whole Earth and 23 years of remodeling a farmhouse, Reizan describes refuge as home: all things are Buddha, life unfolds in a moral universe, and everything is connected and supported. A two-week hike around the Three Sisters, whose peaks climbers nickname Faith, Hope, and Charity, gives each word a meaning. Reizan closes with a donor's plan for an Earth meditation room, built around a poster of the whole world, which lacked a practice to sustain it, and names the chant as that practice of going home.

sentences.text: You know, this is sort of a story probably everyone has heard at some time or another, where one of some astronauts who had years ago was up in space was reflecting about that moment when they were up there in their space and they happened to look out and see the whole Earth as one entity without any of the visible divisions of countries and borders.
And they sort of got it; they got it that the way in which we divide up our lives is sort of fundamentally flawed and that we really live within a much more unified existence.
It's almost become a new cultural story that we all have.
I was thinking about that, and I've been really into being at home recently.

I've lived at my farm now for 23 years, and I've gone through phases there where sometimes I've had a lot of different sorts of people living there and different groupings, and then sometimes I felt like less at home in my own home.
But recently I'm feeling very at home there, and I was even fantasizing recently about how I could just sort of stay at home all the time.
Wouldn't that be nice?

I remember once working on this farm when I was in college where I was only about five minutes drive from town, but I didn't leave the place except for maybe once in a month; that was just their kind of thing.
Sometime along the way, I heard somebody say something about them, that most of our problems would be solved if people just stayed at home.
We're pretty mobile creatures, and the rest of the world is probably pretty confused by us because they're all at home—the trees, the animals, they're all at home, we're running around.

In fact, I'm a building contractor, so I go to other people's homes every day, different places, never the same place all the time, and I spent a lot of time and energy making other people's homes really nice, like down to the last little thing, because that's the way they want it.
And then I come home to my home, where I think I said I was living there for 23 years.
I've been remodeling it for 23 years, so it's not done, not close.
It's an interesting set of feelings to have about life.

Tonight I'm going to be talking about another in a series of talks that we've been doing about the chance in our book, and we're sort of taking it from the beginning and moving through, so I think we're on page two.
I'm talking about the three refuges in Pauley, and this is a chant that we traditionally do at the very end of the day in our Soto Zen tradition.
If we were doing a retreat, it would be right before we went to bed.
And we do it in the Pauley, in the old language, and as a sort of an honoring to the Buddhist tradition, deep and beyond our own.

For this talk, I didn't really do that kind of scholastic research where I tried to translate the words or find out why we do this little song that we do when we sing it, but I think it's quite traditional; I think it's old, and it's a real honoring of our tradition to do that.
It's almost like we do a sort of sing a little bedtime prayer to ourselves, and so it's really sweet.
We'll do it at the end of the evening; it's a chant that is an expression of our sense of Buddhist as what our home is, what our true home is.
And that's why we call it refuges, with very much the meaning that we commonly ascribe to that word.
This is a place of safety in the tumult of life where we are buffeted around through our insecurities and doubts about ourselves, about the world, reality.
This is a place where we can settle, and so it's an important teaching in Buddhism.

Originally, this chant was a sort of existed within a monastic tradition, and so probably had primarily a kind of a sectarian sort of connotation to it—a reaffirmation of basic tenets of doctrine to say, "Yes, I am a Buddhist; I'm reaffirming my Buddhist identity."

But it is also quite possible, and I think more commonly, you know, can be seen today as in wider context, and strictly seeking speaking those those doctrinal aspects of Buddhism should be seen in a pretty wide context because
they don't truly have the type of meaning unless they are applied widely, and you'll see what I'm trying to say here in a minute with that.

But it really comes down to the idea that Buddhism, in a sense, has no real creation mythology like many other religions—the idea that at some time something happened where the world came into being and there were all sorts of manifest meanings about that coming into being that we now look at and learn from.
Because in the Buddhist concept of things, everything is always coming into being and has been, and there was no beginning to that.
So in that sense, having a creation mythology doesn't make a lot of sense in Buddhism.
Instead, we sort of reaffirm that continual coming into being, which is right here and right now, and is our home.
In chanting the refuges, we're giving an expression of faith in a Buddhist context that we are each Buddha, that all things that we call things are Buddha.
If we see something as a thing separate from any other thing, then that's Buddha; that's what we mean by taking refuge in Buddha, because we are affirming this aspect that all things are Buddha.
If we imagine that just "I am Buddha," or just "we are Buddhas," then it's really not taking refuge in Buddha because Buddha is not separate, not two, so that's why all things are Buddha.
And when you affirm that all things are Buddha, that's taking refuge in Buddha.
We take refuge in Dharma in that we recognize that we exist in a moral universe.

It's probably occurred to most of you that there seems to be a striking similarity between ethical codes amongst many different religions, and there's a reason for that: it's because there are commonalities about morality.

An ethical universe isn't really a universe of rights and wrongs; it's a universe of guiding principles you try to live by and carry forward because you find that when they get transgressed, things don't go so well.
Yet you don't really know where the borderlines of those ethical rules really are until you cross them, so it's a lived thing.

Taking refuge in the idea that this is an ethical universe means that you really are taking responsibility for that outside of just how it affects you; you're taking responsibility for this because this is how life is.
Taking refuge in Sangha is a recognition that we are connected and supported; it is not a matrix of isolation.
We literally have no ability to have any sort of life as we know it outside of our connections to other life.
Even within our bodies, millions of bacteria and other life that are essential, we live symbiotically with.
We breathe in oxygen, which has been breathed out by plants, and we walk on the earth; it supports us.
If it wasn't there, we'd be an avoid.
There's almost any infinite number of ways in which we can imagine that we live in a connected and supported situation in this life.
And yet, we often imagine that just the opposite is true.
However, if we would really try and think about how is it possible for me to be completely separate and isolated, it's really actually very, very hard to figure out how that's true at all.
Yet, at some times, it seems as though we have a distinct problem in remembering these three things; it seems as though we often don't remember that we're connected and supported.
We imagine that maybe right and wrong is something I can fudge with here and there in my life.
What's the difference?

We might imagine that, "Well, I don't really realize anything; I'm, you know, Buddhas, and, you know, wise people know so much more than me; I'm just barely trying to figure it out," so we can set up that kind of situation for ourselves.
But when we chant this chant, we're really affirming the opposite; we're affirming all of these things that we often have a difficult time affirming.

This chant and the whole process of taking refuge, which is very core to Buddhism in almost all of its schools, is also really reflected also in the tenth precept of our system of ethical precepts, sometimes referred to as not defaming the three treasures, also referred to kind of in a more positive sense as cherishing and polishing the three treasures.

When I first was studying the precepts, I saw a lot of depth initially in precepts related to refraining from killing, promoting life, refraining from stealing, promoting generosity, refraining from lying, promoting telling the truth, etc.

And I do admit that when I first encountered this precept, I often thought that it felt to me like it might have been something the constructors of a religion would tack in there to sort of prop up their shtick, "Oh, and by the way, don't disregard how important Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are."
But now I sort of see it a little differently; I kind of see it as more of a core ethic that underlies many other ethical concerns because it's sort of a whole universal ethic.
In fact, you could even see it perhaps as standing like a foundational environmental ethic.

Not defaming the three treasures is like not wasting natural resources because not defaming the three treasures in a sense is to not make less of them than what they really are, which is a totalistic description of our existence—that all things are Buddha, that this entire life we live in exists within a moral universe, and that at every point all things are connected and supported.
And this is a sort of an environmental ethic that is exactly the kind of thing that perhaps our society should contemplate a little more seriously and has perhaps left off.
I often think about the Declaration of Independence, the sort of founding principle of our country, founded on the principle of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
Sounds pretty good.
It's often pretty much also interpreted as an individualistic type of ideal, and it doesn't really say anything about being responsible to anything or anybody else.
So I often think that a lot of what's going on with our country and how we exist in the world maybe is because we left out a couple things in the beginning in how we put together our ethical system.

So exploring these three refuges, Buddha, of course, we immediately think of the historical Buddha in this regard; taking refuge in the Buddha, and it might be that we also bring quite a bit of cultural mapping from other religious systems onto that statement in terms of a kind of a bowing down to a historical figure.
But we can also see it in a very wide context, too, and the same can happen with Dharma and Sangha.
We can imagine these as being Buddhist Dharma and a Buddhist Sangha.

And in many ways, these things are great treasures, and we feel that as we practice more how important having a construction, a faith called Buddhism, having teachings and having a group that supports our practice is very important to us.
But I think, you know, for me, it wouldn't be enough.

It wouldn't be enough if I didn't also imagine that there is a great sort of ever-present realization that the world that is always coming into being is trying to become something, as Suzuki Roshi would say, and that there are principles of guidance and support at every turn.
These are the things that I think are going to carry us through when we really need it most.
This last September I took a hike.
We went down to Oregon, and in fact, one participant is here.
We hiked for two weeks and circumambulated three 10,000-foot peaks in the Three Sisters wilderness.
The peaks, North, Middle, and South Sister, are three volcanoes, and climbers have given them nicknames kind of based on the relative difficulty of climbing the mountains.
North they call Faith, Middle is called Hope, and South is called Charity.
South is a mountain that any really reasonably strong hiker can hike up and down in a day, and many people do; it's a walk-up mountain.
Hope, well, you have to be a little more careful there and make sure you don't go off the route, and you have more glacier travel involved.
It's still not too difficult.
Faith, now this is a mountain that you've got to watch out for and should have no business on unless you really know what you're doing.
We hiked around these mountains and we were studying the Three Treasures, and it was avoidable to have some affinity between what we were studying and the Three Mountains.
Taking refuge in Buddha, Dharma, Sangha is a sort of expression of faith in the Buddhist context.
So in that sense, there are different ways to explore what that means.
Faith, in this sense, I think could be something where you just put your trust in openness, have an open-minded, open-hearted acceptance towards life.
Faith, you don't have to have to figure it out, but you can open yourself to being at home with this world.

Hope is perhaps when life really seems to be contradictory and is throwing you some curveballs and just doesn't seem to be adding up in the way it seems as you're due because you've been a good person and you've been trying your best, but have hope that it's going to pay out in the end that you're headed in the right direction anyway.
So you rely on the idea that your life is moving in the right direction and that it will work.
Charity, charity is when good things happen to you and you're not sure how you deserve that; it just came.
Life is good to you sometimes; it's like grace.
And sometimes you feel like, "Did I really deserve all this?"
But accepting that is sometimes the bigger challenge than to accept that life is good.
We chant these and we call it taking refuge or flying home to refuge.
There might be other ways to translate some of these words, but they're so beautiful in and of themselves that it seems better to just leave them as they are.
We might not be getting the meaning exact anyway, and even if we did, it would only be sort of in our mind, and this is all part of practice.

I was thinking about how when we moved into this building, originally there was a person who liked what we were doing and came forward and gave us a lot of money and wanted to see that this happened, which was really a great gift.
She herself had some ideas too about how she wanted to support and extend something into the world, Earth meditation, she called it.
And we built the room that's now the library specifically for that purpose.
And it didn't end up working out in the end.
She had an idea that she would have a poster that was like what the astronauts saw, just that big picture of the world, the whole world, and it seemed like that was a great idea.
It almost seemed like that was just enough right there.
But I think in the end, there wasn't quite enough going along with all that to sustain it; it needed to have a little something about how you practiced with that.
And essentially, this chant is that practice; it's important to have a practice, to have a way of going home.
And we have to practice it because we're constantly becoming.
We're Buddha, right?
So we're always going home; we're always becoming something.
So it's not something you get to do once; it's something we continue to do and we continue to do.
So I think perhaps I'll finish the talk and chant the refuges for the end of the evening.
